node.label: Allan Greer
node.date_label: “Fur-Trade Labour” 1981 · “A Critique of Pentland” and Peasant, Lord, and Merchant 1985 · Colonial Leviathan (ed. with Radforth) 1992 · The Patriots and the People 1993 · Property and Dispossession 2018 · “Settler Colonialism and Beyond” 2019
node.description: A historian of Lower Canada and colonial North America whose rural social history described a feudal, household-centred habitant society: in 1985 he held that Lower Canadian 'agriculture was organized primarily around the satisfaction of family subsistence needs through family production', with part of the surplus 'diverted to priests and seigneurs through feudal exactions', a view he set against both Ouellet's routine-bound peasant (1981) and the commercial farmer of Paquet and Wallot, while allowing that 'Feudal peasants or market-conscious farmers? No doubt the debates will continue' (1985). The same essay, a critique of Clare Pentland's Labour and Capital in Canada, faulted the staples tradition of Innis and Creighton for confining attention to 'relations of exchange'. With Ian Radforth he edited Colonial Leviathan (1992), on mid-nineteenth-century state formation, which Bryan Palmer found to lack coherence (1993) and which Greer later said 'neglected everything to do with Indigenous peoples and processes of elimination' (2019); his history of the 1837 rebellion (1993) is known here through reviewers, who read it as breaking with Ouellet's manipulated peasantry. His later work on 'property formation' (2018) and his 2019 lecture treat settler colonialism as one mode of colonial invasion among several, 'a dominant force in some periods and regions' that 'fades to insignificance in others', while insisting 'I am not here to trash or dismiss settler-colonial theory'.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Allan Greer (b. 1950); “Fur-Trade Labour and Lower Canadian Agrarian Structures” (1981); “Wage Labour and the Transition to Capitalism: A Critique of Pentland” (Labour/Le Travail, 1985); Peasant, Lord, and Merchant: Rural Society in Three Quebec Parishes, 1740–1840 (1985); ed. with Ian Radforth, Colonial Leviathan: State Formation in Mid-Nineteenth-Century Canada (1992); The Patriots and the People: The Rebellion of 1837 in Rural Lower Canada (1993; French translation Habitants et Patriotes, 1997); “Commons and Enclosure in the Colonization of North America” (2012); Property and Dispossession: Natives, Empires and Land in Early Modern North America (2018); “Settler Colonialism and Beyond” (2019).
node.scope_note: This entry presents Greer's account of rural Lower Canada and the transition to capitalism (1981–85), the state-formation collection (1992) and his later historicising of settler colonialism (2018–19). Read on 2026-10-14: 'Wage Labour and the Transition to Capitalism' (1985, pp. 7–22) and 'Settler Colonialism and Beyond' (2019, pp. 61–86) in full; the introduction to Property and Dispossession (2018, pp. 1–24) on Cambridge Core, which shows no page markers; Palmer's 1993 review of Colonial Leviathan in full. 'Fur-Trade Labour' (1981) was read in full for the Ouellet entry and its critique of Ouellet is carried by edge_989, not repeated here. Peasant, Lord, and Merchant (1985) and The Patriots and the People (1993) are unread (lending-only copies); the 1985 book is known from its publisher's description and the 1993 book from reviews. Ouellet's review essay on the 1993 book (Histoire sociale / Social History, 1995) is unread, so no reply by Ouellet is quoted. His New France and Jesuit work (The People of New France, 1997; Mohawk Saint, 2005) is not covered.

proposed_edges.relationship: Rural Lower Canada as a feudal, household-centred peasant society, neither routine-bound nor market-rational, into which wage labour in the fur and timber trades was fitted (1981–85); and the rebellion of 1837 as a rural popular movement (1993, known through reviews)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: His own words (Labour/Le Travail 15, 1985, read in full): 'my own view is that agriculture was organized primarily around the satisfaction of family subsistence needs through family production. There were surpluses and a portion of these were sold, but a significant proportion was diverted to priests and seigneurs through feudal exactions' (pp. 18–19); against the commercial reading of Paquet and Wallot, cited in n. 16, 'Feudal peasants or market-conscious farmers? No doubt the debates will continue', while 'none of these social formations were dominated by the capitalist mode of production' (p. 19); 'capitalist enterprise had to adapt itself to the prevailing non-capitalist environment' (p. 20); subdivision of holdings followed 'the introduction of domestic industry or of seasonal waged work in the fur or timber trades' (p. 16). Peasant, Lord, and Merchant (1985) is unread; its publisher describes rural Quebec as 'essentially organized around a feudal society', with 'a pronounced pattern of household self-sufficiency' in three Lower Richelieu parishes (lof_greer_1985). His 1981 Sorel study rejected the 'atavistic mentality' explanation of the rural crisis; that critique of Ouellet is carried by edge_989 and is not repeated here. The Patriots and the People (1993) is unread. Reviewers' words, not his: Dessureault (1998, read for evidence-quebec.md) says it 'brise nettement avec les travaux antérieurs de William H. Parker et de Fernand Ouellet pour qui la paysannerie était essentiellement victime de la crise économique et manipulée par des élites ultranationalistes', finds the struggle fed by 'une forme de républicanisme populaire' (p. 206), places Greer 'dans une perspective marxiste anticolonialiste, héritière de l'œuvre pionnière de Stanley B. Ryerson' (p. 205) and objects that he 'réfute l'existence de clivages socio-économiques à l'intérieur même de la paysannerie' (p. 207); Cardinal (1999) writes that 'à plusieurs reprises, A. Greer s'en prend aux arguments de cet historien' (p. 185). Ouellet's review essay on the book (Histoire sociale / Social History 28, 1995) is unread (browser check), so his reply is not quoted and no fernand_ouellet edge is drawn. Rudin (1995) names Greer among the révisionnistes.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: No single strand fits: agricultural_crisis_debate holds him for the 1981 critique (edge_989) and rebellions_1837_interpretations for the 1993 book. Retarget to rebellions_1837_interpretations if the editor drops the 1985 half.
proposed_edges.roster_row_note: His quebec_historiography row (historian, 1.138) describes the 1981 Sorel study, Peasant, Lord, and Merchant (1985) and the 1993 rebellion history: this intervention.

proposed_edges.relationship: Colonial Leviathan (1992, edited with Ian Radforth): mid-nineteenth-century state formation in the Canadas, written before the framework was named, and later faulted by Greer himself for neglecting Indigenous peoples (2019)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Colonial Leviathan is unread (lending-only copy; the Érudit, Left History and Histoire sociale reviews returned bot checks). In-period reading: Palmer (Labour/Le Travail 31, 1993, read in full) says the volume and Curtis's book 'are searching for the state in pre-Confederation Canada' (p. 365) and finds that 'the collection lacks coherence', while its 'single most important contribution ... also developed by Curtis, is the notion that the coming of ‘responsible government’ actually entailed the subversion of the reform strategy of the 1830s' (p. 366); he names Greer's chapter on the birth of the police (p. 366). Valverde's 1992 essay cites Fecteau's chapter in the volume (edge_966). Greer's own later judgment (2019, read): 'The time may be right, then, for a renewed history of the Confederation era, one that unites the history of state formation with that of settler colonialism' (p. 73), with n. 41: 'A prime example of this problem would be Colonial Leviathan; devoted to questions of state formation, it neglected everything to do with Indigenous peoples and processes of elimination' (p. 84). Comparison only: the volume predates McKay's prospectus (2000), and no checked text by McKay or his commentators names it; Pâquet (2009) links the framework to studies of state formation in general. The atlas's state_formation_roots strand places it there editorially.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: state_formation_roots ('State formation before the framework') holds Greer, Radforth and lof_greer_radforth_1992. Drawn as a comparison, like Valverde's edge_966 to the same strand, because no checked text joins the volume to McKay's framework; the editor may prefer contribution, as for Curtis.
proposed_edges.roster_row_note: His liberal_order_framework row (historian) names Colonial Leviathan among three interventions (Peasant, Lord, and Merchant; Colonial Leviathan; commons and property formation). The row covers this edge in part; the editor may leave its edge_id empty.

proposed_edges.relationship: Settler colonialism historicised as one mode of colonial invasion among several, beside imperial/commercial penetration and extractivism, dominant in some periods and regions of northern North America and not others: a sympathetic critique that keeps Wolfe's 'structure, not an event' (2018–19)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: His own words, all after 2000 and dated. 'Settler Colonialism and Beyond' (Journal of the CHA 30, 2019, read in full; a CHA keynote): settler colonial theory 'does indeed have much to offer historians', but over 500 years of invasion 'the settler variety stands out as a dominant force in some periods and regions, but it fades to insignificance in others' (p. 62); 'The late Patrick Wolfe, still the most important theorist of settler colonialism' (p. 62); the danger of 'temporal flattening' 'when settler colonialism is casually invoked in ways that suggest a transhistorical, always-already quality' (p. 63); 'Let me assure you that I am not here to trash or dismiss settler-colonial theory' and, with Wolfe, settler colonialism is 'a structure, not an event'; 'However, that doesn't mean we need to find settler colonialism everywhere and all the time' (p. 63); 'Imperial/Commercial Penetration' and 'Extractivism' are 'coexisting and overlapping versions of colonialism' (p. 64); early settlements 'hardly functioned as instruments of elimination and replacement except in quite limited, localized ways' (p. 64); 'To those who insist that Canada is, was, and always has been a settler-colonial phenomenon, I offer qualified support' (p. 73); 'settlers as such are no longer the main threat, for the invasion has adopted a different guise' (p. 74); and 'Settler colonialism stands out also as a fundamental force behind the creation of a territorial nation-state' (p. 79). Property and Dispossession (2018), introduction read on Cambridge Core (no page markers): 'Some scholars speak of an “eliminationist” logic driving settler colonialism ... toward the utter destruction of natives who stand in its way', but 'such “ethnic cleansing” is not the whole story' (n. 25 cites Wolfe 2006). The target is the field, not patrick_wolfe: Greer accepts Wolfe's structure thesis and objects to how the term is commonly used, citing Woolford and Benvenuto's warning that it risks becoming 'a reductive shorthand' (p. 63). The William and Mary Quarterly essay (2019) is unread beyond its recorded opening.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: critiques_and_limits ('regional and periodic fit with other modes of colonialism (Greer)') holds him and both 2019 sources.
proposed_edges.roster_row_note: His settler_colonialism row (critic) states this argument.

proposed_edges.relationship: In a critique of Pentland's Labour and Capital in Canada, the staples tradition's trade-centred economy faulted for confining attention to relations of exchange and passing over the household subsistence production that, he argued, made up most of early Canada's economy (1985)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: His own words (Labour/Le Travail 15, 1985, read in full), in a critique of H. C. Pentland's Labour and Capital in Canada, 1650–1860 (written 1960, published 1981), which is not an atlas entry: Pentland 'follows the lead of his Toronto mentors in conflating the Canadian economy and its overseas trade'; 'While Innis, Creighton, and their contemporary disciples confine their attention to relations of exchange, however, Pentland at least focuses on the ‘social relations of production’', so 'it seems fair to regard him as the labour historian of the staples school' (p. 9). The subsistence producers who were most of the population 'were therefore scarcely of interest to bourgeois theorists from Adam Smith to Harold Innis and Clare Pentland. For these last two, ‘the colonial economy’ meant the meagre flow of commodities' (p. 21). His counter-claim is stated as an untested estimate: 'No one has yet made a serious attempt to measure the value of the colony's annual production of all goods'; 'If they did, I have no doubt that the aggregate agricultural output would embody vastly more labour than all the furs and squared timbers and other ‘staple products’' (p. 20). Qualifications kept: Pentland 'deserves high marks for posing the important questions and for assembling valuable information' (p. 8). The arrow stands for this passage of a review essay aimed chiefly at Pentland; Greer names Innis and Creighton as the staples school but does not review their books. Note 2 (p. 8) also discusses Kealey's and Palmer's use of Pentland; that is not drawn as an edge.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: staples ('Development read through the export of raw materials') holds Innis and the staple sources; Greer names 'Innis, Creighton, and their contemporary disciples'. Not targeted at harold_a_innis because Greer addresses the school, not Innis's books.
proposed_edges.roster_row_note: Greer has no cdn_national_tradition row; roster_additions proposes one (critic), linked to this edge.

new_sources.title: Allan Greer, “Wage Labour and the Transition to Capitalism: A Critique of Pentland,” Labour/Le Travail 15 (Spring 1985): 7–22.
new_sources.citation: Allan Greer, “Wage Labour and the Transition to Capitalism: A Critique of Pentland,” Labour/Le Travail 15 (Spring 1985): 7–22.

verification.note: Read in full (pp. 7–22) in the journal's own PDF (lltjournal.ca article 2454, galley 2857; scanned with a text layer, also OCR'd locally; folios from the running heads). Passages used: Pentland's work is 'a fundamentally incoherent book' and 'neglects the broader context needed to grasp this general transformation' (p. 9); Pentland 'follows the lead of his Toronto mentors in conflating the Canadian economy and its overseas trade' and 'While Innis, Creighton, and their contemporary disciples confine their attention to relations of exchange, however, Pentland at least focuses on the ‘social relations of production’', so 'it seems fair to regard him as the labour historian of the staples school' (p. 9); subdivision of holdings resulted from 'the introduction of domestic industry or of seasonal waged work in the fur or timber trades' (p. 16); Pentland's ethnic argument belongs to 'an ambivalent but, in the end, predominantly liberal, view of the advent of capitalism' (p. 18); 'my own view is that agriculture was organized primarily around the satisfaction of family subsistence needs through family production. There were surpluses and a portion of these were sold, but a significant proportion was diverted to priests and seigneurs through feudal exactions' (pp. 18–19); 'Feudal peasants or market-conscious farmers? No doubt the debates will continue' and 'none of these social formations were dominated by the capitalist mode of production' (p. 19; n. 16 cites Paquet and Wallot 1972 for the commercial view); 'capitalist enterprise had to adapt itself to the prevailing non-capitalist environment' (p. 20); Pentland's neglect of the household economy 'inevitably leads him to write women out of his history' (p. 20); 'If they did, I have no doubt that the aggregate agricultural output would embody vastly more labour than all the furs and squared timbers and other ‘staple products’' (p. 20); subsistence producers 'were therefore scarcely of interest to bourgeois theorists from Adam Smith to Harold Innis and Clare Pentland' (p. 21). Note 2 (p. 8) discusses Kealey's and Palmer's readings of Pentland, calling Palmer's Working-Class Experience an 'otherwise excellent synthesis'. Note 14 announces Peasant, Lord and Merchant as forthcoming.

new_sources.scope_note: Greer in his own words on the pre-capitalist household economy of early Canada, the transition to capitalism and the staples tradition.

new_sources.title: Bryan D. Palmer, review of Bruce Curtis, True Government by Choice Men? (1992), and Allan Greer and Ian Radforth, eds., Colonial Leviathan (1992), Labour/Le Travail 31 (1993): 365–367.
new_sources.citation: Bryan D. Palmer, joint review of Bruce Curtis, True Government by Choice Men? Inspection, Education, and State Formation in Canada West (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 1992) and Allan Greer and Ian Radforth, eds., Colonial Leviathan: State Formation in Mid-Nineteenth Century Canada (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 1992), Labour/Le Travail 31 (1993): 365–367 (in the issue's 'Reviews / Comptes Rendus' section, pp. 365–433).

verification.note: Read in full (pp. 365–367) in the journal's own PDF of the reviews section (lltjournal.ca article 4891, galley 5764; scanned pages with a text layer; folios 365, 366 and 367 printed in the running heads). Passages used: 'THESE BOOKS are searching for the state in pre-Confederation Canada'; 'In their purpose they can only be applauded; but their search is at times disturbingly narrow' (p. 365); Curtis 'telescopes the process of state formation in Canada West in the 1840s into the emergence of educational inspectors' and 'this study is too minutely focused' (p. 365); the promotional claim that Curtis 'presents a systematic application of the insights of ... Marx, Weber, Durkheim, Gramsci, and Foucault' (p. 365); as a 'model' Curtis's account 'is overstated to the point of distorting actual historical relations in the evolution of state and civil society' (p. 366); 'the collection lacks coherence' (p. 366); 'The single most important contribution of the articles in this collection, also developed by Curtis, is the notion that the coming of ‘responsible government’ actually entailed the subversion of the reform strategy of the 1830s' (p. 366); the gender essays read as 'complementary to the revisionist assessment of ‘responsible government’ as an expression of a slight [sic] of hand that promised popular sovereignty at the same time as it delivered institutionalized subordination and regulation' (pp. 366–367); 'Books like these make the job easier' (p. 367). Palmer names Greer's chapter on the birth of the police (the text layer prints the name as 'Allan Green's', p. 366).

new_sources.scope_note: In-period critique of Curtis's inspection study and of Colonial Leviathan, by the atlas's Bryan Palmer. Used in the Curtis and Greer entries.

screq_greer_2019_jcha.note: Read in full for the 1.139 Allan Greer person entry (Érudit PDF served to an ordinary request; text layer; folios 61–79, notes 80–86). Based on a keynote address to the CHA annual meeting (first-page note). Passages used: settler colonial theory 'does indeed have much to offer historians' but 'the settler variety stands out as a dominant force in some periods and regions, but it fades to insignificance in others' (p. 62); 'The late Patrick Wolfe, still the most important theorist of settler colonialism' (p. 62); the hazard of 'temporal flattening' 'when settler colonialism is casually invoked in ways that suggest a transhistorical, always-already quality, as though the settler-colonial condition had no discernible beginning and as if it could never end' (p. 63); 'Let me assure you that I am not here to trash or dismiss settler-colonial theory. I personally think it has a great deal to offer anyone trying to understand the present and the past of a country such as Canada' (p. 63); historians 'need to take on board the critique of settler-national historiography sketched out by Wolfe and developed more fully by others such as Lorenzo Veracini' (p. 63); 'However, that doesn't mean we need to find settler colonialism everywhere and all the time' (p. 63); 'My objective is to try to historicize settler colonialism' (p. 63); 'Imperial/Commercial Penetration' and 'Extractivism' as 'coexisting and overlapping versions of colonialism' (p. 64); early settlements 'hardly functioned as instruments of elimination and replacement except in quite limited, localized ways' (p. 64); settler colonization 'emerged as an important independent force' only from the last quarter of the eighteenth century (p. 70); 'The time may be right, then, for a renewed history of the Confederation era, one that unites the history of state formation with that of settler colonialism' (p. 73), with n. 41: 'A prime example of this problem would be Colonial Leviathan; devoted to questions of state formation, it neglected everything to do with Indigenous peoples and processes of elimination' (p. 84); 'To those who insist that Canada is, was, and always has been a settler-colonial phenomenon, I offer qualified support' (p. 73); 'settlers as such are no longer the main threat, for the invasion has adopted a different guise' (p. 74); 'Settler colonialism stands out also as a fundamental force behind the creation of a territorial nation-state' and 'An order based on territorial dispossession is not, and never has been, normal, natural, and inevitable' (p. 79). The source's page range 61–86 includes the notes.

lof_greer_2018.note: Introduction (chapter DOI 10.1017/9781316675908.001, pp. 1–24) read for the 1.139 Allan Greer person entry on Cambridge Core, whose HTML shows no page markers, so no page locators are given; quotations were taken in short segments. Passages used: the book 'deploys the concept of “property formation”'; it challenges the view 'that sees property as a single thing, the hallmark of civilization and modernity'; 'In spatial terms, dispossession is really the essence of colonization'; 'Some scholars speak of an “eliminationist” logic driving settler colonialism ... toward the utter destruction of natives who stand in its way', but 'such “ethnic cleansing” is not the whole story' (n. 25 cites Wolfe 2006); 'there is still an unreflexive tendency to equate colonization and modernization'. A passage on a 'leftist variant' linking colonization and capitalism quotes, unnamed in the text, Cronon's Changes in the Land (n. 6, p. 77 of Cronon).

pe137_ouellet_greer_1993.note: OpenAlex record (publisher summary, not Greer's words): the book looks 'into the actions, motives, and mentality of the rural plebeians who formed a majority of those involved in the insurrection' and 'brings to light new causes for the revolutionary role of the normally peaceful French-Canadian peasant'. Book still unread.
